outputs.L1:
The present invention relates to a ship-collision prevention system and method for preventing a collision between a ship at sea and another ship. More particularly, the invention provides a ship-collision avoidance guidance system employing a time-series graphical display.

To address the shortcomings of conventional electronic chart display and information systems (ECDISs) and navigation systems using such ECDISs—particularly their complex and unintuitive screen displays resulting from the mere enumeration of various items of information—the guidance system graphically displays, in time-series form, changes over time in the relative distances to respective ships and obstacles, based on information provided by the ECDIS and a radar system. For each ship, the system uses radar information to indicate whether the ship is located on the port or starboard side. If the distance to a particular ship is equal to or less than a predetermined threshold, the system issues an alarm or other notification directing the ship obligated to keep out of the way to take avoidance action.

Accordingly, the system enables users to readily identify, at a glance, the positions of nearby ships and obstacles at sea, the timing of crossing events, and whether a particular ship is to be avoided. The system thereby effectively prevents collisions between ships at sea while also enabling simulations of crossing events and avoidance maneuvers through the input of arbitrary values.
outputs.L2: The invention concerns a system and method for avoiding collisions between a vessel at sea and other vessels. It provides collision-avoidance guidance through a time-series graphical display. Conventional electronic chart display and information systems (ECDIS) and related navigation systems often present numerous data items as a simple list, resulting in complicated, non-intuitive screens. To address this issue, the proposed system uses information obtained from ECDIS and radar equipment to graph changes over time in the relative distances between the vessel and individual ships or obstacles. For each detected ship, radar data is also used to indicate whether it is located to port or starboard. When the distance to a particular ship falls to or below a preset threshold, the system issues an alarm or similar notification directing the vessel that is required to keep out of the way to take avoidance action. Consequently, users can readily determine the locations of nearby vessels and obstacles, the expected time of a crossing event, and which vessel must maneuver to avoid collision. The system therefore helps prevent maritime collisions effectively while also allowing crossing and avoidance scenarios to be simulated by entering arbitrary values.

The invention provides a ship-collision avoidance guidance system based on a time-series graphical display. The system receives navigation data from an Electronic Chart Display and Information System (ECDIS) and radar equipment, then uses this information to plot changes in the relative distance between the vessel and nearby ships or other obstacles over time.

Radar data is also used to determine whether each nearby vessel is located on the port or starboard side. When the distance between vessels falls below a predetermined threshold, the system identifies the vessel that is required to give way under the applicable navigation rules and issues an alarm to prompt appropriate evasive action.

By presenting the relevant information in an intuitive graphical format, the system enables operators to identify obstacles and nearby vessels at a glance, estimate potential crossing times, and determine the respective collision-avoidance obligations of the vessels involved. In addition to processing real-time navigation data, the system supports simulations based on manually entered values, allowing users to assess hypothetical encounter situations and evaluate possible avoidance maneuvers in advance.
outputs.L4:
The invention relates to a ship-navigation support system designed to make collision risks easier and faster for bridge crews to understand. Conventional electronic chart display and information systems (ECDIS), radar screens, and automatic tracking displays often present large amounts of information through symbols, vectors, numerical values, and multiple overlapping targets. Although these systems provide essential navigational data, their displays can become complex and unintuitive, particularly in congested waters or when several vessels are approaching from different directions. As a result, an operator may have difficulty immediately determining which targets present the greatest danger, when a crossing will occur, or which vessel has the obligation to keep out of the way.

To address these limitations, the invention obtains positional and movement information from ECDIS, radar, and, where available, other onboard sources such as an automatic identification system. The collected information may include the own ship’s position, heading, speed, and course, together with corresponding information for nearby vessels, fixed structures, coastlines, shoals, and other obstacles. Based on these data, the system calculates or continuously updates the relative distance between the own ship and each selected target.

Rather than displaying only a plan-view map or a set of numerical closest-point-of-approach values, the system presents the relative distance as a time-series graph. The graph allows an operator to see whether the distance to a target is increasing or decreasing, how rapidly the target is approaching, and when the minimum separation or crossing point is expected to occur. Present, historical, and predicted values may be shown together so that changes in risk can be recognized at a glance. Multiple targets may be plotted simultaneously using different colors, line types, symbols, or labels.

The display further indicates whether each vessel or obstacle lies on the port side or starboard side of the own ship. This directional information may be represented by the position of a plotted line, a divided display region, an icon, a color, or another visual indicator. The operator can therefore understand not only the magnitude and trend of the relative distance, but also the side from which the target is approaching. Such information is particularly useful when determining whether a situation constitutes a head-on encounter, overtaking, or crossing and when applying applicable right-of-way and give-way rules.

The system may also provide a simulation function for evaluating future navigation scenarios. Using the current courses and speeds of the own ship and surrounding vessels, the system predicts their relative movement and displays an anticipated crossing time, closest point of approach, or distance at the closest point of approach. A crew member may enter or select a proposed course or speed change, after which the system recalculates the predicted tracks and updates the time-series graph. In this way, alternative collision-avoidance maneuvers can be compared before they are carried out. The display can show whether a proposed maneuver increases safe separation, creates a new risk with another target, or conflicts with navigational right-of-way obligations.

Hazard levels may be determined according to preset or user-defined distance and time thresholds. If the relative distance to a vessel or obstacle falls below a specified value, or if a predicted closest approach is unsafe, the system generates an alarm. The alarm may include visual highlighting, flashing symbols, audible warnings, or prioritized messages identifying the relevant target and the nature of the danger. Different warning levels may be used to distinguish an emerging concern from an immediate collision risk. Thresholds may also be adjusted according to vessel size, speed, maneuverability, visibility, traffic density, or the characteristics of the navigational area.

By converting relative-motion information into an intuitive time-series representation, the invention reduces the cognitive burden placed on bridge personnel. Crews can more readily identify hazardous targets, estimate crossing times, determine whether another vessel is passing to port or starboard, and recognize which vessel must take avoiding action. The simulation and alarm functions further support timely and informed decision-making. Accordingly, the invention improves situational awareness and assists in preventing collisions and other navigational accidents at sea.

# The ECDIS: Modern Navigation at Sea

The Electronic Chart Display and Information System (ECDIS) is a computer-based navigation system used on ships. It displays digital nautical charts and combines them with information from onboard equipment such as GPS, radar, speed logs, and the Automatic Identification System (AIS).

ECDIS helps navigators plan routes, monitor a vessel’s position, and identify potential hazards. The system can provide warnings when a ship approaches shallow water, restricted areas, or other dangers. When used with official Electronic Navigational Charts (ENCs), an approved and properly maintained ECDIS may replace traditional paper charts.

However, ECDIS does not eliminate the need for skilled navigation. Officers must understand chart settings, safety parameters, alarm functions, and the limitations of digital information. Charts and software must also be kept up to date. Incorrect settings, outdated data, or excessive reliance on automation can create serious risks.

The ECDIS has made maritime navigation more efficient and has improved situational awareness on the bridge. Nevertheless, its effectiveness depends on accurate information, proper maintenance, and well-trained users.

counterfactuals.output: A ship-collision avoidance guidance system is disclosed that integrates electronic chart display and information system (ECDIS) data with radar-derived target data to provide graphical situational awareness and maneuvering guidance. The system acquires own-ship position, course, and speed, charted obstacle information, and detected or tracked target-ship parameters. A processing unit determines relative distances between the own ship and nearby ships, shorelines, navigational structures, shallow-water boundaries, and other obstacles over a selected past or predicted time interval. The determined relative distances are presented as time-series graphs on a display, enabling an operator to identify closing trends, minimum-distance events, and collision risks. The graphs may include closest point of approach, time to closest point of approach, safety thresholds, target identifiers, and predicted distance curves corresponding to candidate course or speed changes. The system may generate visual or audible alerts and recommend avoidance maneuvers when a distance trend crosses a configurable safety criterion, thereby supplementing conventional ECDIS and radar presentations with readily interpretable temporal guidance.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an English patent abstract for a “ship-collision avoidance guiding system using a time series graphic display,” emphasizing the shortcomings of existing navigation screens, relative-distance plotting, obstacle tracking, alarms, and crossing-event simulation.
counterfactuals.output: A ship-collision avoidance guiding system using a time-series graphic display is provided. Conventional navigation screens primarily present instantaneous vessel positions, headings, and radar echoes on a geographic or relative-motion plot, making it difficult for an operator to intuitively recognize changes in relative distance, identify developing collision risks, distinguish tracked obstacles, or predict the sequence and timing of crossing events. Existing closest-point-of-approach alarms may also be issued too late, generate excessive nuisance warnings, and fail to explain how an encounter will evolve. The disclosed system receives own-ship navigation data and tracking data for one or more target ships or obstacles, calculates relative distance, bearing, approach rate, closest-approach parameters, and predicted crossing information, and plots the calculated information along a common time axis. Historical, current, and predicted values are displayed as continuous graphic traces, with respective targets visually identified and risk thresholds indicated. The system tracks changes in each obstacle’s motion, generates graded visual and/or audible alarms when a trace enters a predetermined danger region, and updates the display in response to course or speed changes. A simulation function models alternative own-ship maneuvers and graphically presents resulting crossing times, passing distances, and risk states. Accordingly, the operator can compare encounter trends and proposed avoidance actions without relying solely on a congested plan-view screen.
